reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: An interstitial deletion of the proximal long arm of chromosome 18, distinct in phenotype from the more common distal (terminal) 18q deletion
Developmental delay and intellectual disability, generally with prominent behavioural difficulties
Seizures appear to be more frequent than in the distal deletion
Growth and stature are relatively less affected, and the characteristic aural atresia and dysmyelination of the distal deletion are typically not the dominant features
Hypotonia and variable, often non-specific, dysmorphism may be present
The clinical picture depends on the precise interstitial segment lost and which dosage-sensitive genes are involved
Recurrence risk depends on whether the deletion is de novo or reflects a parental rearrangement
Chromosomal microarray defines the deletion and distinguishes it from the distal 18q deletion
reference.pathophysiology: Proximal 18q deletion syndrome arises from an interstitial loss within the proximal long arm of chromosome 18, sparing the terminal segment. As a contiguous-gene disorder, its features result from haploinsufficiency of the particular dosage-sensitive genes contained in the deleted interval, which differ from those lost in the distal deletion; this accounts for the distinct phenotype, with a greater tendency to seizures and behavioural disturbance and relatively less effect on growth and hearing. The variability in the position and size of the interstitial deletion explains the heterogeneity between individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Distal (terminal) 18q deletion syndrome, which has a different clinical profile
Other interstitial deletion syndromes causing developmental delay and epilepsy
Idiopathic or other genetic epilepsy syndromes
Idiopathic autism spectrum disorder and behavioural disorders
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray as the first-line test to detect and size the interstitial deletion and distinguish proximal from distal 18q involvement
FISH or MLPA to confirm the deletion and assess for a parental rearrangement
Parental studies to exclude an inherited rearrangement and counsel recurrence risk
EEG and neurological assessment where seizures are present or suspected
Brain MRI and other targeted imaging where clinically indicated
redFlags: Feeding difficulty or faltering growth in infancy
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals have intellectual disability of variable degree with behavioural challenges, and seizure control is often an important determinant of function. With appropriate developmental, educational and neurological support, many reach adulthood, though the outlook varies with the extent of the deletion and the severity of epilepsy and behavioural problems.
pitfalls: Conflating the proximal deletion with the distal 18q deletion, whose growth, hearing and imaging features differ
Underestimating the seizure burden and failing to arrange appropriate neurological assessment
Attributing behavioural problems solely to the deletion without structured support
Omitting parental studies where an inherited rearrangement is possible
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
